messages.subject: Extract percentile values?
parts:
Hi all;
Suppose that we run a hypothetical simple model and the as you know the estimation output is as follow:

------------------------------------------------
> fit
Inference for Stan model: model.
1 chains, each with iter=10; warmup=5; thin=1; 
post-warmup draws per chain=5, total post-warmup draws=5.

      mean se_mean   sd  2.5%   25%   50%   75% 97.5% n_eff Rhat
mu   -0.06    0.08 0.17 -0.27 -0.12 -0.12  0.11  0.12     5 0.76
lp__ -6.85    0.06 0.13 -7.00 -6.96 -6.87 -6.72 -6.72     5 0.76
-----------------------------------------------


How to extract the percentile value (for example 0.12) and save it to a vector for further work on it. 
Note that I want to replicate the model and save the values to a vector.

Best Regards
Mahdi

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Extract percentile values?
parts:
No, they are empirical percentiles estimated from the MCMC
draws.  In particular, the 2.5% and 97.5% estimates are very
very noisy and we do not recommend using then to estimate
a HPD interval.  A 5%-95% interval is relatively robust but a
10%-90% is even better while still giving you a good idea of
the posterior concentration.

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Extract percentile values?
parts:
Unfortunately there is little literature on the estimation of quantiles
from samples, but you see some of the issues in Andy’s paper,
http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/HPD_STCO.pdf.

The biggest challenge with these quantile estimators is that it’s
hard to assign confidence intervals because they’re not quite
expectations and hence don’t quite fall into MCMC central
limit theorems.  But if you don’t believe me then simulate it
yourself — start with IID gaussian draws and see how many
samples it takes to accurate pin down the extreme quantiles.

On May 26, 2016, at 3:24 PM, Mahdi Akbarzadeh <akbarz...@gmail.com> wrote:

Then what is the confidence coefficient for that? (5%-95%)?
Can you introduce a reference for the statement?

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Extract percentile values?
parts:
I think you guys may be talking past each other.

I think Mahdi's asking for how you assign confidence
to a parameter estimate, not how you calculate confidence
intervals for MCMC estimators of quantiles (though I
am interested in hearing more about the answer to that
question given that they're not expectations).

Mahdi --- those posterior intervals are Bayesian and any text
on Bayes should explain what's going on. They are not
highest posterior density intervals, just central ones. And
by all means do what Michael suggests in terms of pinning down
extreme quantiles. We should have that in a tutorial somewhere.

- Bob

messages.author: f53f4ca2c430170d
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Extract percentile values?
parts:
On Thursday, May 26, 2016 at 10:37:36 AM UTC-4, Michael Betancourt wrote:
limit theorems.  But if you don’t believe me then simulate it
yourself — start with IID gaussian draws and see how many
samples it takes to accurate pin down the extreme quantiles.

Or don't do it yourself but take a look at a very basic script here: 
https://github.com/sakrejda/stan-workshop/blob/master/odsc-10-quantile-estimation.R

K
On May 26, 2016, at 3:24 PM, Mahdi Akbarzadeh <akbarz...@gmail.com> wrote:

Then what is the confidence coefficient for that? (5%-95%)?
Can you introduce a reference for the statement?
On Thu, May 26, 2016 at 6:35 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:

No, they are empirical percentiles estimated from the MCMC
draws.  In particular, the 2.5% and 97.5% estimates are very
very noisy and we do not recommend using then to estimate
a HPD interval.  A 5%-95% interval is relatively robust but a
10%-90% is even better while still giving you a good idea of
the posterior concentration.
On May 26, 2016, at 2:28 PM, Mahdi Akbarzadeh <akbarz...@gmail.com> wrote:
These values are percentiles of the parameter posterior distribution. I use them as HPD intervals (0.025 and 0.0975).
On Thu, May 26, 2016 at 2:43 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:

Note that these yield MCMC _estimates_ of the posterior quantiles,
not exact values.  In particular, quantiles below 5% and above 95%
are notoriously hard to estimate and the estimators will be really
noisy.
On May 25, 2016, at 3:41 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:

On Wednesday, May 25, 2016 at 5:01:22 AM UTC-4, Mahdi Akbarzadeh wrote:
Hi all;
Suppose that we run a hypothetical simple model and the as you know the estimation output is as follow:

------------------------------------------------
> fit
Inference for Stan model: model.
1 chains, each with iter=10; warmup=5; thin=1; 
post-warmup draws per chain=5, total post-warmup draws=5.

      mean se_mean   sd  2.5%   25%   50%   75% 97.5% n_eff Rhat
mu   -0.06    0.08 0.17 -0.27 -0.12 -0.12  0.11  0.12     5 0.76
lp__ -6.85    0.06 0.13 -7.00 -6.96 -6.87 -6.72 -6.72     5 0.76
-----------------------------------------------


How to extract the percentile value (for example 0.12) and save it to a vector for further work on it. 
Note that I want to replicate the model and save the values to a vector.
 
The print() method does not return anything, so I think your best bet would be

sapply(as.data.frame(fit), FUN = quantile, probs = 0.25)

Ben
